articles.title: Jim Harbaugh is in unfamiliar territory ... and the Chargers are in trouble
articles.summary: The Chargers are 0-2, and the schedule only gets harder from here.
articles.body:
It's always fun when a tumbling boulder from the chaotic avalanche that is college football bounces into the well-manicured lane of the NFL. The characters that dominate college football's frenetic Saturdays don't always translate so well to the NFL's choreographed Sundays.

Jim Harbaugh has won at the professional level, leading the 49ers to the Super Bowl after the 2012 season. But the man is college football through and through, from his khakis to his weird one-liners, and right now he's looking a whole lot more fit for Saturdays than Sundays.

Harbaugh's Chargers are 0-2 after losses to the Cardinals and Raiders — the Cardinals! the Raiders! — and although we're just two weeks into the season, matters are already bordering on dire. Why? Well, let's start with the most obvious sign: their schedule.

From here into November, the Chargers face the Bills (away), Seahawks (away), Broncos, Chiefs (away) and Rams (away, sort of), with a blessed bye week after Kansas City . Damn! You couldn't script a more difficult five-game sequence if you tried!

The odds are stacked against teams that start 0-2 making the playoffs — roughly 10 percent since 1990, per research from NBC Sports — but teams that start 0-7? Yeah, you don't need to consult ChatGPT for that one. There's a very real chance the Chargers are winless into November.

It wasn't supposed to be this way. Harbaugh's Chargers were supposed to be angling for a division championship and a run at a Super Bowl. With Justin Herbert at quarterback and Mike McDaniel as offensive guru, the Chargers were, in theory, headed for Bills-Chiefs territory, sustaining elite performance and silencing the last of the doubters.

The doubters are now at jet-engine volume. The hyped-to-the-moon offense hasn't even gotten off the launching pad, ranking below league averages in both ground and air attacks. The only teams with two games played averaging fewer than the Chargers' 14 points per game? Miami , Pittsburgh and Atlanta . That's a stink that won't come out.

Sunday's game against Las Vegas — predicted to be among the NFL's worst teams; there's a reason they had the No. 1 pick — was a perfect example. The Chargers mostly couldn't move the ball, and when they did, they turned it over.

"That's not up to our standard," Herbert said afterward, and while that's a nice lie to tell yourself in the locker room, the truth is that your standard is on the scoreboard, not the feeling you have in your hearts. And right now, the Chargers' standard is garbage.

"It wasn't good enough," Harbaugh said. "There's no time for us to be patient with how we were playing. It's not good enough, so we have to be better."

Sure, that's the right thing to say. But can they be better? The league has been waiting for Herbert, 0-3 in the playoffs, to level up for half a decade now. McDaniel was drawn to this job rather than another head coaching one because of Herbert's possibilities.

But McDaniel's highly complex offensive schemes rely, first and foremost, on the quarterback getting rid of the ball quickly. Herbert is more of a deliberate pocket passer; in 2025, per NFL NextGen Stats , his release time was 2.9 seconds, 32nd among NFL quarterbacks. McDaniel said in the preseason that he hoped to get that release time down to 2.4 seconds; after two games, Herbert's release time stands at … 2.8.

"How smart is Mike McDaniel and Justin Herbert? I can't tell you because I'm not smart enough to know how smart those two are," Harbaugh joked during a preseason interview . "But the more they're together … Justin understanding Mike, and Mike [understanding] Justin, it bodes really well for the Los Angeles Chargers."

Or not. Harbaugh is now in unfamiliar territory; he's never started a season, college or pro, at 0-2. His team is a turnover-laden mess, sitting at -4 already this season, including three interceptions from Herbert. Harbaugh's usual motivational speeches aren't working, but Harbaugh is attempting to salvage the season one sound bite at a time.

"I'm not deterred," he said Sunday afternoon. "No one in that locker room is deterred."

History offers Harbaugh and the Chargers one tiny bit of hope: Only one team has ever started the season 0-4 and reached the playoffs. Back in 1992, that team rallied to win 11 of their final 12 games, claim their division and even win a playoff game. That team? The San Diego Chargers.

Or, if you're particularly sadistic, think of it this way. "Chargering" is the term this franchise inspired for moments when you implode spectacularly on the national stage — like, say, blowing a 27-point playoff lead . But hey, you can't go Chargering off the side of a mountain if you never even climb that mountain in the first place, right?

articles.title: The NFL says Guardian Caps make football safer. The science isn't so sure
articles.summary: Guardian Caps have become one of football's most visible attempts to reduce concussions. But as the NFL embraces them as a safety measure, scientists are sti...
articles.body:
After enduring four concussions in his first three NFL seasons, Chris Olave decided he could no longer justify prioritizing swag over safety.

The New Orleans Saints receiver has begun wearing a Guardian Cap over his helmet on game days in hopes that the cartoonishly bulky, foam-padded covering offers better protection against blows to the head.

"Shoot, I got kids now," Olave told reporters earlier this month after his team's season opener against Detroit . "I want to live a regular life after I'm done with football. I love my kids to death. So, I don't really care how it looks no more. I just got to throw it on."

For football players, the dangers of strapping on a helmet and stepping between the white lines have never been clearer. Scientists have demonstrated that the cumulative effect of repeated blows to the head is the most reliable predictor of what could cause someone to suffer from the degenerative brain disease known as chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.

At least 1 in 4 former NFL players who died from 2016-2021 had CTE, according to a recent study published in the British Medical Journal, and researchers say that 25% estimate represents a conservative floor. The prevalence of CTE among deceased former NFL players has only further ratcheted up the pressure on the league to show that it's proactively hunting for answers.

Since 2022, the NFL has touted the innovation of a mom-and-pop duo as a potential solution. NFL officials have cited lab tests showing that the Guardian Cap cushions the impact of hits to the head by at least 9%. They also point to a roughly 50% reduction in concussions when players wear the extra layer of padding over their helmets during practices.

Those figures are the NFL's rationale for requiring players to either wear a Guardian Cap during contact practices or one of the handful of helmet models that have performed best during safety tests. The league has also permitted the use of Guardian Caps during games since the start of the 2024 season, though Olave is one of just a few dozen players who have risked social media ridicule by wearing one on a game day.

"We think it has been a step forward for player safety overall," said Jeff Miller, the NFL's executive vice president for health and safety initiatives.

And yet not all independent neurologists and neuroscientists support America's most powerful and visible sports league throwing its weight behind the Guardian Cap. Some expressed concern that Guardian Caps give athletes a false sense of security without meaningfully reducing the risk of CTE. Others cited a 2025 study involving the NFL's top medical official that poked holes in the league's claim associating Guardian Caps with a decrease in concussions.

Providing further fuel for criticism is the fact that the Guardian Cap NXT model worn by NFL and Division I college players is not the same as the product marketed to the masses. The lighter-weight XT model, which sells for as much as $89.99, has less padding than the NXT. Impact tests conducted by multiple different laboratories have shown that the XT model may be less effective than the NXT at protecting the head and reducing injury risk.

"The jury is out on whether the Guardian Cap is helping NFL players," said Chris Nowinski, co-founder of Boston University's CTE Center and one of the world's most renowned figures in brain injury research. "We have no reason to believe it's helping high school and college players.

"We've created a sort of nightmare scenario where people strap these things on their kids' helmets and believe they're now safe from concussions and CTE. Nothing could be further from the truth."

The story of the Guardian Cap actually begins about a quarter century before its invention.

In fall of 1987, an industrial designer from Erie, Pennsylvania, was watching a college football game and witnessed a particularly brutal helmet-to-helmet collision. The jarring hit inspired Bert Straus to try to devise a product capable of cushioning the impact of such blows.

Several years of tinkering produced the Pro Cap, an energy-absorbing, half-inch foam shell that attached to the top of a conventional football helmet. Former Buffalo Bills free safety Mark Kelso credited the Pro Cap for extending his NFL career by a few years. So did former San Francisco 49ers left tackle Steve Wallace.

Unresolved questions about the Pro Cap's effectiveness contributed to the NFL never fully embracing it, as did pushback from players reluctant to wear a bulky, goofy-looking product. The concept gradually faded from football despite repeated attempts from Straus to revive it.

By 2010, Straus sought help developing a helmet with a soft, energy-absorbing exterior capable of withstanding repeated hits without cracking or becoming ineffective. Straus approached Lee and Erin Hanson, an Atlanta couple whose material sciences company specialized in developing custom polyurethane formulations for anything from body shields for the U.S. Army to the outer layer of golf balls.

For Erin Hanson, helmet safety was an issue that felt deeply "personal." The mother of five had a son who had started playing football. Her father was a coal miner's son who used football to earn a full ride to Purdue and hoist himself out of poverty.

"In my family, football is everything," Hanson said. "There are so many benefits to having kids involved with football, but I wanted to find a better, safer way to do it."

At the onset of the NFL's concussion crisis, with the league facing criticism over its callous approach to brain injuries, commissioner Roger Goodell organized a summit of helmet safety experts to discuss possible reforms. Straus and Erin and Lee Hanson traveled to a hotel ballroom in Manhattan in December 2010 to pitch their product in front of Goodell and members of the NFL's head, neck and spine committee.

The presentation, Erin Hanson admits, was not well-received. The soft-shell helmet prototype was "too ahead of its time," she said.

"We were told that this will never fly, that we were taking the sound out of the game," Hanson added. "That made sense to people who wanted to hear the sound of helmet shells cracking, I guess, but I really did not want to hear my son playing like that."

The failure to gain traction only made the Hansons more determined. They struck out on their own, convinced that the best market opportunity lay not with redesigning the football helmet but with creating a protective add-on that addressed some of the most frequent complaints about Straus' Pro Cap.

The Guardian Cap was lighter weight and designed to fit any helmet because it attached with clips or straps. It also shifted and slid atop a helmet rather than affixing directly to it, redirecting impact without increasing neck torque, according to laboratory tests that the Hansons paid for to vet their product.

"We knew that we could make a difference if someone would give it a try," Erin Hanson said, but early believers were hard to find. Entire days would pass at football trade shows or sports medicine conventions without the Hansons' booth attracting more than a few visitors.

Potential customers were especially scarce at one 2013 conference in Destin, Florida.

"It was crickets all day Friday and all day Saturday," Erin Hanson recalled. "On Sunday, Lee and I said, 'We're just going to walk into the town and get lunch because nobody's coming to our booth.' "

Shortly after the Hansons returned to pack up and head home, a man approached their booth and said, "Well, that makes perfect sense." That man was orthopedic surgeon Jeffrey Guy, team physician for the University of South Carolina athletic department. His enthusiasm was the breakthrough the Hansons had long been seeking.

The NFL hops on board … but not the players

At Guy's recommendation, Jadeveon Clowney and the rest of the South Carolina football team started wearing Guardian Caps during their 2013 summer practices. Then in-state rival Clemson followed suit. Before long, Guardian Caps were showing up on high school and college practice fields across the country, and the NFL was displaying newfound interest.

In April 2017, the Hansons received a grant of $20,000 from the NFL to support testing of the Guardian Cap at Biocore, an NFL-funded biomechanics and injury prevention research lab in Charlottesville, Virginia. The lab tested the lone existing version of the Guardian Cap at the time — the one the Hansons were selling to high school and college programs — but the 7-ounce XT model scarcely reduced the severity of impacts experienced by NFL players.

"They didn't really withstand much more force, if any, than helmets alone," said Miller, the NFL's executive vice president for health and safety initiatives. "Now they may work for other levels of the sport, but they certainly weren't working at the speeds and forces that NFL players are subjected to."

The Hansons responded by creating the more heavily padded NXT version of the Guardian Cap, which fared considerably better in testing. Biocore attached the 12-ounce Guardian Cap NXT to a variety of different helmets, placed the helmets on the head of a crash-test dummy and fired a mechanical impactor into it at different angles and speeds. The NXT model decreased head impact severity by 9% compared to just the helmets alone. When both dummies wore the NXT model, the force of a helmet-to-helmet collision was nearly 20% less severe.

Encouraged by those results, the NFL permitted the use of Guardian Caps in practice in 2020 and mandated their use by certain position groups two years later. On Sept. 8, 2024, Steelers guard James Daniels and Patriots safety Jabrill Peppers became the first players to wear the protective helmet covering in a regular-season game.

To say that the Guardian Caps were unpopular among fashion-conscious NFL players is a massive understatement. Miami Dolphins linebacker Jordyn Brooks described Guardian Caps as "UFO caps." Arizona Cardinals defensive end JJ Watt told reporters , "You feel like a bobblehead." Philadelphia Eagles center Jason Kelce protested by showing up to his first 2022 training camp practice with bubble wrap around his helmet.

Among the few players who endorsed the change was offensive lineman Justin Pugh , who tweeted , "Let's laugh at how dumb we look but increase our chances of remembering our kids' names."

The barrage of jokes about the clunky-looking Guardian Caps hasn't prevented the Hansons from cashing in on the NFL's endorsement of their product. Sales for Guardian Caps have surged the past few years, with over 500,000 athletes worldwide now wearing the protective helmet covering.

To Erin Hanson, those sales figures are a success story. To others, they're something else entirely.

Researchers: The NFL's math isn't mathing

If the NFL marketed the Guardian Cap as a way to slightly improve a player's odds of avoiding a brain injury, Nowinski insists he wouldn't put up a fuss.

The former Harvard defensive lineman and advocate for football safety says he only began speaking out when Roger Goodell repeatedly trumpeted the product as having "reduced concussions by 50%" despite evidence to the contrary.

In 2024, a group of researchers, including NFL chief medical officer Allen Sills, reviewed league surveillance footage to analyze the impact of Guardian Cap use on the concussion rate during preseason practices from 2018 to 2023. They reviewed video of every concussion to determine which players were involved in the collision and whether the cause was a blow to the helmet shell.

The results of the study suggest to Nowinski that the NFL was premature in giving the Guardian Caps credit for reducing the concussion rate by 50% rather than considering the potential role of other variables. When only concussions involving helmet shell impact were considered, the study found that "there was no longer a significant relationship between Guardian Cap use and the incidence of concussions."

"When the peer-reviewed study showed that it wasn't the Guardian Cap that was reducing the rate of concussions, the NFL didn't do anything to correct itself," Nowinski said. "How unethical is it to go trumpet this massive reduction in concussions that sells half a million Guardian Caps to kids, giving them a false sense of security of concussion prevention, and then not correct yourself when the study comes out?"

The company that designs and manufactures Guardian Caps stands behind their effectiveness in reducing the impact of hits to the head but makes no claims about concussions. On the Guardian Sports website, the Hansons include a disclaimer that reads in part, "No helmet, headgear or chin strap can prevent or eliminate the risk of concussions or other serious head injuries while playing sports or otherwise."

The NFL's stance remains largely unchanged. While Miller says the NFL endorsed the Guardian Cap because of its ability to decrease the severity of head impact, he did not shy away from the league's previous concussion-related claims.

"Look, the players who wore the Guardian Cap saw the concussion reduction and those that didn't [wear the Guardian Cap] didn't," Miller said. "So I have to attribute at least some of the concussion reduction to the Guardian Cap."

How effective Guardian Caps are at insulating football players from other dangers is also a complicated topic.

In 2024, researchers at Virginia Tech's helmet-testing laboratory found that players who wear the Guardian Cap's NXT model experience an 8% decline in linear accelerations and a 14% decline in rotational accelerations. That suggests to Virginia Tech helmet laboratory director Steve Rowson that the NXT model "may be helping a little."

"It's really hard to quantify the effect in the real world," Rowson said, "but when we're starting to see reductions over 10%, that stands out."

The benefits were significantly less from the Guardian Cap XT version worn by youth and high school players. The average reduction in linear acceleration was just 3% and in rotational acceleration was just 5%.

Decreasing the severity of blows to the head by such a small amount "isn't meaningfully reducing the risk" of CTE, according to Daniel Daneshvar, chief of brain injury rehabilitation at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital and associate professor at Harvard Medical School. In fact, the way Daneshvar sees it, the NXT model's head impact figures "aren't going to make a huge difference" either.

The average force of a routine blow to the head in a high school football game is 27 times the force of gravity, according to Daneshvar. An 8% reduction, Daneshvar points out, is still nearly a 25G impact. A 3% reduction is still an impact of more than 26G.

"You're much better off taking that 27G impact and making it a 0G impact by modifying the way that you practice," Daneshvar said.

Multiple brain injury experts expressed concern that neither the Hansons nor the NFL is doing enough to clarify that the version of the Guardian Cap worn by professional football players is not the same as the model available for the public to purchase.

"I would guess that less than 1% of people realize that," Nowinski said.

When asked if he found that problematic, Miller said the NFL's focus "has always been developing a model that works for us and sharing that data."

"I can't say that we've spent time testing other versions of the Guardian Cap at speeds that the lower levels of the sport engage in," Miller added. "I guess that would ultimately be a question for the company to see what they've done in that regard."

Erin Hanson pushed back against the notion that the NXT model of the Guardian Cap is a "completely different product" than the XT.

"It's got an extra layer so it's a little bit heavier," she said, "but it's doing the same reduction of impact at NFL speeds that we're getting with our product at lower speeds for the youth level."

Since Lee and Erin Hanson first came up with the design for the Guardian Cap 15 years ago, helmet technology has steadily improved. Instead of having biomechanical engineers test whether helmets met a minimum safety standard, the NFL began asking labs to assess which helmets reduced impact severity the most.

The byproduct has been a competitive marketplace in which a helmet that was once considered state-of-the-art could be substandard within a few years. Newer helmets feature flexible or deformable shells, multiple layers and densities of foam and position-specific padding designed to protect players where data suggests they get hit the most.

"It wasn't until helmets started getting rated, both by us and the NFL, that manufacturers were incentivized to try to make the best performing helmet possible," Rowson said. "These evaluation systems really accelerated innovation in the helmet space. Helmet manufacturers, rather than relying on their own data, could then point to independent data to show why their helmet is better at reducing risk."

Top-performing helmets are already performing well enough that Rowson wonders if there will be a market for the Guardian Cap or other helmet shell add-ons in 5-10 years. The advantage to strapping a Guardian Cap to a top-tier helmet today is far more marginal, Rowson said, than it was just a few years ago.

That's a stance the NFL and NFLPA shares. Already the league is incentivizing players to pick the safest available helmets by telling them they'll no longer have to practice in Guardian Caps as a result.

"I see the Guardian Cap as a transitional piece of equipment," Miller said. "Meaning that if the technology in the helmets continues to improve at the pace that it is right now, that will push players to the better-performing helmets, as opposed to the Guardian Cap.

"Now that said, Guardian Cap could come up with a new device that adds much more benefit. I'm sure they're working on that but the helmet manufacturers are making great strides at a really rapid pace. Therefore we're very comfortable encouraging players to wear those helmets where the Guardian Cap becomes optional."

To Nowinski, the Guardian Cap may have already outlived its usefulness. He has friends who regularly ask him if they should buy one for their kids.

"I always say no," Nowinski said. "There is no evidence they make your kids safe."

articles.title: Mike Macdonald says Sean Payton accused team of cheating after Seahawks used fan videos to scout Denver's offense
articles.summary: Fan videos are becoming a popular scouting tool among NFL coaches.
articles.body:
When NFL training camp starts next season, coaches might want to be careful about what plays they run in front of fans. Thanks to the era of social media, videos from team training camps are more prevalent than ever … and that exact issue nearly led to some significant cheating accusations going public a few years ago.

Seattle Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald revealed Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton grew furious with the Seahawks in 2024 and eventually threatened to publicly accuse the team of cheating.

Payton apparently believed the Seahawks employed SpyGate-like strategies or went into full Connor Stalions mode to steal signals from the Broncos before a game. As Macdonald explained during an interview with Graham Bensinger, Seattle's method was much simpler — and did not break any NFL rules.

To get an edge on their Week 1 opponent in 2024, the Seahawks scouted fan videos of plays the Broncos ran during training camp.

The tactic worked, as the Seahawks won the contest 26-20, giving Macdonald his first-ever win as an NFL head coach.

But once Payton got word that the Seahawks had his plays, he reportedly grew furious at Seattle general manager John Schneider. Macdonald claimed Payton vowed to make his accusations public, at which point the Seahawks told the coach they would sue him over making false allegations. Macdonald said that was enough to get Payton to back down.

It's not the first time fan videos have come under scrutiny this season. In early September, Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said opposing teams were using fan videos from training camp to do advance scouting.

While that was likely never the intention of teams that open training camp to the public, it's not something that can really be curbed under the current format. Once a video hits social media, it's public information. The NFL can't ask opposing coaches not to look at something that's widely available.

But repeated stories of this ilk could result in teams cracking down on videos being taken during training camp. If NFL teams don't want to go that route — or find it too hard to police — coaches may start to get even more conservative when the public is watching practice.

If Macdonald's story confirms anything, though, it's that NFL coaches will do whatever it takes to get an edge. And if that means someone spends a day dissecting oddly angled fan videos to determine what route a team's X receiver runs out of a specific formation, that's fine. It's well worth the information gained in the end.

Swift announced her new single "Patient Zero" will be available on Friday.

Tuesday's announcement comes after the famously eagle-eyed Swifties noticed the pop-music superstar had changed the written lyrics on streaming platforms from some of her already-released music to replace the letter "O" with the number "0" in spots.

"Patient Zero" will mark Swift's first new release since her wedding to Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce on July 3. It will be her second single of the year after "I Knew It, I Knew You" from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack.

There is no confirmation of a full album at this point, but Swift has released at least one album every year since 2019. This includes re-recordings of her old albums.

articles.title: Tom Brady Explains How Eliminating Negative Plays Elevated Josh Allen’s Game
articles.summary: Speaking with Colin Cowherd on “The Herd," seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady broke down Josh Allen’s development.
articles.body: Through two games, Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen is playing like a guy ready to add another MVP trophy to his mantle. After leading the Bills to a 2-0 start, Allen is off to one of the strongest statistical openings of his career. He’s thrown for 582 yards and five touchdowns while adding another 92 yards and four scores on the ground. These impressive numbers also come without Allen throwing an interception. Speaking with Colin Cowherd on "The Herd," seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady broke down Allen’s development. He immediately focused on Allen’s development under Brian Daboll before he left to take the New York Giants head coaching job. "I thought there was a lot of development that took place when he had Brian Daboll as his [offensive] coordinator," Brady said. "I think he learned the system. He’s got an awesome ability to improvise and we’ve seen that for a long time." Beyond Allen’s physical traits, Brady pointed out that his ability to avoid negative plays has been his biggest area of growth. Early in his career, turnovers were a frequent criticism, but Allen has turned his play on the field into a far more disciplined decision-maker. "He’s got the big arm, the legs and can kind of run the big plays," Brady said. "It’s always been ‘how can he eliminate the negative plays?’ The bonehead fumbles, the bonehead sacks and those plays are the ones that put your team behind the eight ball." articles.title: Matthew Stafford Moves to Sixth on NFL’s All Time Touchdown List!
articles.summary: Matthew Stafford continues to climb the NFL record books. During the Los Angeles Rams’ 28-6 victory over the New York Giants on Monday night, Stafford moved...
articles.body:
Matthew Stafford continues to climb the NFL record books.

During the Los Angeles Rams ' 28-6 victory over the New York Giants on Monday night, Stafford moved into sixth place on the NFL's all-time career passing touchdown list. His 11-yard touchdown pass to Davante Adams in the third quarter gave him his 426th career touchdown pass, moving him past Philip Rivers .

The veteran quarterback threw four touchdown passes overall against New York, finishing the night with 427 career touchdown passes. He completed 22 of 31 attempts for 327 yards and one interception while leading the Rams to their first victory of the season.

The milestone was fittingly part of an outstanding night for Stafford and Adams. Two of Stafford's four touchdown passes went to Adams, who exploded for eight catches, 195 yards and two touchdowns.

Stafford's first touchdown of the night came on a 10-yard pass to Kyren Williams before he connected with Adams twice. His fourth touchdown went to tight end Terrance Ferguson late in the fourth quarter.

The performance marked the 22nd time in Stafford's career that he has thrown at least four touchdown passes in a game. It also helped the Rams bounce back from their 27-7 season-opening loss to the San Francisco 49ers.

Stafford's latest milestone adds another impressive accomplishment to a career that has already included an Super bowl, multiple Pro Bowl selections and numerous league records.

At 38 years old, Stafford is continuing to add his name to some of the NFL's most prestigious statistical lists. With 427 career touchdown passes and plenty of football still ahead, his climb through the record books is far from over.

A wellness check on the NFC North after two weeks doesn't give particularly optimistic results. The Detroit Lions ' defense is in major trouble and the issues might not be easily fixable. The Chicago Bears ' defense isn't much better, and the offense feels a little more vulnerable after scoring only three points in Week 2. The Green Bay Packers ' defense has been average but the offense might be falling apart at the seams.

The Vikings are undefeated despite getting 11 snaps from Kyler Murray so far this season. He is expected to return from a concussion in Week 3 . At this point it might not matter who the quarterback is.

The Vikings allowed three points to a Bears offense that was the talk of the NFL after scoring 59 in Week 1. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores is proving to be a mad scientist. He blitzed Caleb Williams on 27 of his 33 dropbacks (81.8%), according to Next Gen Stats. A week ago, the Vikings blitzed on 40 of Jordan Love 's 46 dropbacks (86.9%), according to Pro Football Focus. At this point opponents should assume Flores is blitzing at about an 80% rate, which is astonishing in the NFL. But it has been successful.

The Vikings' offense hasn't been good. It's last in the NFL in yardage gained. But presumably Murray will be better than Carson Wentz . And the Vikings are 2-0 with both wins coming in division games already as their offense catches up.

There's a lot of season to go, but the Vikings are in good shape. Don't forget they were 14-3 two seasons ago with competent quarterback play and 9-8 last season without it. Perhaps everyone should have taken the Vikings more seriously coming into the season. If Murray can play at an average level, perhaps Minnesota is surprisingly the best team in the NFC North? They're certainly in the best shape early this season, even if by default.

Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 2 of the NFL season:

The Dolphins are the only team in the NFL that has not led at any point through the first two weeks of the season, according to Doug Clawson of CBS . On Sunday, they trailed the 49ers 35-6 before a meaningless touchdown in the final three minutes. The Dolphins were fairly competitive in the first half, trailing just 14-6 at halftime, but were outscored 21-0 in the third quarter.

"We didn't coach well enough in the second half," Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said . "We didn't play well enough. I thought we had a great week of preparation. I thought we were ready to play better. Second half, not good enough in any phase."

The Dolphins' next three games are against 2-0 teams: vs. Chiefs , at Vikings, vs. Bengals .

The Falcons' passer rating through two games is 38.2. If a team threw incomplete on every single play, their passer rating would be 39.6. Michael Penix Jr. has not been a good quarterback yet in his young career, but compared to what the Falcons have put on the field there might be a parade in Atlanta upon the news that he'll start this week against the Packers . Perhaps Penix will play well. He'll certainly be better than Cooper Rush or Jack Strand, and he'll make Atlanta at least watchable on offense. The Falcons play their next three games in prime time for some reason, including Thursday night at Green Bay. There's a lot of time for the Falcons to salvage their season, but it's overly optimistic to believe Penix is a savior. Atlanta's biggest problem has been quarterback, but it's not the only problem.

The Titans aren't in the business for moral victories, but at least they were way more competitive in Week 2 against a talented Eagles team. They led until the Eagles scored the game-winning touchdown with nine seconds left. There will be many regrets. The Titans had first-and-goal at the 9-yard line with 2:37 left on the clock and the game tied, and right tackle JC Latham got immediately beat by Jalen Carter for a 9-yard sack. Tennessee settled for a field goal, giving the Eagles an opening to steal the win. At least everything looked better, including Cam Ward (13 of 20, 183 yards) against a very good defense.

"I think what encouraged me the most was that we were able to get some explosive offense," Ward said .

The Cardinals' longest reception Sunday was 9 yards. That's a stat about the Seahawks more than anything, but it was the first time since Oct. 11, 1987 that the Cardinals didn't complete a pass for at least 10 yards, via Theo Mackie of the Arizona Republic . That game came with replacement players during a player strike. That won't be Arizona 's offense all season, but it is weird how the Cardinals refuse to use Jeremiyah Love more. The third overall pick of the NFL Draft had nine carries for 29 yards, Tyler Allgeier has 22 carries this season and Love has 20. Love might be limited due to a high ankle sprain in preseason, but it makes very little sense why the Cardinals would use that kind of draft capital on a running back and then underutilize him. There's hope for Love emerging, which might not the case for Marvin Harrison Jr. , who has one catch in two games.

There wasn't a great chance that Geno Smith was going to drive the Jets for a win in 50 seconds if Aaron Glenn called a timeout and forced the Packers to punt near the end of regulation. But his explanation, that he was worried about being pinned deep after a punt, doesn't make much sense either.

The Jets are clearly better than last season. They won at a Titans team that was much more competitive in Week 2 against the Eagles, and they led the Packers 17-7 in the fourth quarter. They held the Packers to 199 yards and that counts overtime. But the Jets need to close these games out or Glenn's job security will continue to be an ongoing conversation.

It's strange to see Dan Quinn get criticized for Jayden Daniels dislocating his elbow on the final play of the first half because he went for the touchdown and not the field goal. Going for the touchdown at the 1-yard line when you trail 17-10 is a reasonable football decision. What's unreasonable is calling a game worried about your quarterback getting hurt every play. What happened to Daniels was unfortunate but that's football. The tough part is it's quickly becoming a big part of Daniels' career arc. Since a historic rookie season he played just seven games last season and now is dealing with a dislocated elbow again. The Commanders are 0-2, looked bad on defense against the Cowboys, and now might have to try to save their season with Marcus Mariota presumably filling in for Daniels for a bit.

The last time a team had a start to the season like the Chargers, it was 1926 and that team disbanded one game later. More on those 1926 Racine Tornadoes and the history they now share with the 2026 Chargers, from OptaSTATS:

You don't need 100-year-old comparisons to see the Chargers have been the NFL's most disappointing team so far this season. While one of Justin Herbert 's interceptions Sunday came on a dropped pass that was batted in the air, he has two touchdowns and three interceptions to start the season. Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel hasn't transformed the offense as expected. And now the Chargers have a brutal upcoming schedule . A 2-7 midseason record — or worse — is not off the table.

"I'm angry, but being angry doesn't fix anything," Chargers safety Derwin James Jr. said . "Being angry doesn't fix the problem that we have. We have to get it fixed."

The Buccaneers were 6-2 at their bye week last season, and had a win at Seattle on their résumé. They are 2-9 since and one win came last season against a Cardinals team that went 3-14 last season. Sunday's loss to a Browns team that lost to Jacksonville 34-10 the week before is a new low for Todd Bowles, who suddenly has to be the top candidate to be the first head coach fired this season. The Buccaneers are too talented to lose nine of 11 games since the middle of last season.

"We've dealt with adversity before," Bowles said, via the team's site . "This is an adverse situation again, first time at the beginning of the season but we're 0-2 right now. We've got to pull ourselves up by our boots and we've got to win."

If that seemed like Deshaun Watson 's greatest moment with the Browns, it was, statistically speaking. It was his top EPA per dropback in any game for Cleveland.

Watson had a good second half with the Browns' running game doing nothing. Removing Watson's 22 yards on seven rushes, the Browns rushed for 22 yards on 16 carries. Watson and the Browns' defense were the drivers of this win. Watson clearly did enough to keep his job for another week , and the reaction to him from Browns fans at the home opener will be interesting. At least it's coming off a win and a good performance.

The Steelers' offense was bad against the Patriots and afterward, Aaron Rodgers had what was perceived as a bit of a shot at his coaches.

"In a game like today where there wasn't a lot of flow to it, we need to be better and it starts with me," Rodgers said . "At, like, making sure Mike [McCarthy] knows what's working, what's not working, our coaches know, so we can call stuff we feel like has a better chance."

Even if his words are being twisted, the big problem is the Steelers are trusting a 42-year-old quarterback way too much. The Steelers have 81 passing attempts, which is third in the league, and they're passing about 65% of the time despite not being in pass-only mode much of the season. The Steelers never trailed by more than four points in Week 1 and the game didn't get away from them Sunday until a Rodgers fumble was returned for a touchdown early in the fourth quarter. Mike McCarthy has just made a decision to pass it over and over like it's 2011 with Rodgers. Pittsburgh has one offensive touchdown in eight quarters with that approach.

Bryce Young is second in the NFL with 648 passing yards through two games, only 14 yards behind Tyler Shough for the league lead. Young was also tied for first in the NFL through Sunday's games with six touchdown passes. It has helped to play hapless defenses like the Bears and Falcons, but the production is undeniable. It helps that Jalen Coker was one of five receivers through Sunday's games with more than 200 yards through two weeks. Young is under contract through the 2027 season, and he's starting to make a case for the Panthers to give him a lucrative second contract.

The question is whether Shane Steichen should have gone for it in overtime. In hindsight, giving the ball to Patrick Mahomes when all he needed was a field goal to win was not the right call. But it wasn't an easy call. The Colts had a fourth-and-8 and came out hoping to go for it but got a defensive look that was not conducive to them getting the first down. So Steichen called timeout and took the field goal, hoping his defense could get a stop.

Steichen said he told quarterback Daniel Jones , before the timeout: "If you love it, man, let's go at it. Let's go win this thing. But if it's not the right look ... let's kick the field goal here."

He'll be second-guessed for it after the Colts lost a hard-fought game in overtime. Steichen is under a lot of pressure to show progress and keep his job, and an 0-2 start with a questionable coaching decision isn't an ideal beginning.

Nothing looks good for the Packers right now, especially on offense. The line is beyond banged up and Green Bay lost right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele to a potentially season-ending injury. Receiver Jayden Reed went down with a back injury on the Packers' first drive Sunday. The running game is non-existant without Josh Jacobs . MarShawn Lloyd has been a non-factor and got just six carries Sunday before he was essentially benched after a fumble. Jordan Love had just 145 passing yards against a Jets secondary that was historically bad last season and didn't have Minkah Fitzpatrick . The Packers won in overtime Sunday, coming back from a 17-7 fourth-quarter deficit. If they didn't rally, the panic would be ramped up even more. The Packers are lucky the hapless Falcons are next on the schedule because they have a lot of issues to work through.

The Texans ' run game was dreadful Sunday when it had to carry the offense with receiver Nico Collins out. The Texans had a putrid 6.7% success rate on runs against the Bengals. Only one team has a mark under 20% in a game this season, and that was the Raiders at 18.5% in Week 2. It's stunning that the Texans have not fixed their offensive line issues over multiple offseasons despite it being an obvious liability.

"For us just collectively as a team, the one key to this victory was controlling the front and from an offensive perspective and we did not control their front," Houston head coach DeMeco Ryans said, via Texans Wire. "We got outplayed up front. We couldn't run the ball well. That forced us into a lot of passing situations."

The Texans bounced back from an 0-3 start to make the playoffs last season, but they're in a big hole after losing two home games to begin this season.

Klint Kubiak's offense will get a lot of credit for the Raiders' 2-0 start. While that side of the ball is playing well, it's more notable what Vegas' defense is doing. The Raiders' defense is first in the NFL in EPA allowed per play, and by a wide margin . Part of that (and part of the reason the Raiders aren't higher in the rankings yet) is they've played a Dolphins team that might be on 0-17 watch and a Chargers team that has looked as bad as anyone through two weeks. If the Raiders keep playing like this on both sides of the ball, they'll move up fast. And already, it seems like the free-agent and draft additions have made significant improvements on both sides of the ball.

That's more of what we expected from the Cowboys. Dak Prescott threw four touchdowns, breaking Tony Romo 's franchise record for career TD passes . The offense came alive but the defense is still a question after giving up 389 yards despite Jayden Daniels missing half of the game due to an elbow injury. The Cowboys didn't have a sack. They have two sacks in two games, and the only player with more than a half-sack is safety Caleb Downs . Things will be fine if the Cowboys' offense is putting up 37 points like Dallas did Sunday, but it's hard to win that way in the NFL. It's easier to attack those issues after a win, and team owner Jerry Jones is optimistic.

"We're better than we've been in the last two years on defense," Jones said, according to the team's site . "And offensively, we saw some really impressive things tonight."

The Giants had a scare when Jaxson Dart hurt his knee Monday , and while Jameis Winston is one of the better backup quarterbacks in the NFL, he is also capable of throwing his team out of any game with inopportune interceptions. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that initial exams on Dart indicated he has a sprained MCL, which could cause him to miss some time. If he does, the Giants will be much more volatile. Monday night's loss at the Rams was ugly, as the Giants were outgained 481-182, but losing Dart early affected the whole operation. We shouldn't forget how good they looked against the Cowboys in Week 1.

The Saints are a 2-point conversion away from being 2-0 with road wins over the Lions and Ravens . Given the issues elsewhere in the NFC South, the Saints look like they're the best team in the division. They were the best team in the division over the second half of last season too. There was controversy over whether Tyler Shough scored on a fourth-and-goal quarterback sneak that gave the Saints the lead — it was ruled a touchdown on the field though it wasn't clear Shough broke the plane and was not reversed after a replay review — but the comeback in the fourth quarter on the road against a good Ravens team made it a well-earned win. The next step for New Orleans is not falling behind early and having to make a big comeback.

The fear over Caleb Williams' injury has subsided since it seems like a fairly minor hamstring injury, and yes his extremely distressed reaction to a hamstring strain was odd. At least it wasn't a major injury. What needs to be addressed is how the Bears' offense was inept just one week after putting up 59 points at Carolina. The Bears scored three points against Minnesota and that was with Williams playing three-and-a-half quarters. It would have been better had it not been for a D'Andre Swift fumble at the 1-yard line and a blocked field goal. The rainy weather was certainly an issue, but it's not like the Bears won't be playing more bad weather games. They're still having trouble getting Luther Burden III , Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland (14 combined catches in two games) involved. One bad game doesn't mean the Bears are in trouble on offense, but one great game might not make them the highest scoring offense in NFL history either.

"The weather was a major factor in this game," Bears head coach Ben Johnson said, according to the team's site . "It was the big story of this game. Both defensive coordinators did a great job making it very challenging for the opposing offense. I thought that was the tale of the tape."

The Lions have given up 658 passing yards, which is second-most in the NFL, with only the Colts being worse. They are decimated due to injuries, which is why they were working out defensive backs like Jordan Fuller and Jalen Mills on Monday, according to Jeremy Fowler of ESPN. Safety Avonte Maddox is the latest to go down; he'll miss the rest of the season due to a foot injury. Since halftime of the season opener, the Lions have given up 71 points and 804 yards. Facing Josh Allen in Week 2 factors into the defensive problems, but it's still alarming.

"Defensively, we knew it was a tall task, but we gave up too much," Lions head coach Dan Campbell said . "There were some things in there that we have to get cleaned up. You have to play your best ball to have a chance to reduce points against that team and that quarterback, and we did not do that. We had a hand in helping them out there a little bit, and it wasn't good enough. It's not good enough."

The good news is the Lions still have an easy schedule, and there are winnable games coming up against the Jets, Panthers and Cardinals. Detroit needs to win those games to quell some fears, especially about its defense.

The Broncos' turnaround after six poor quarters to start the season might have been as simple as figuring out how to get Jaylen Waddle and Jonah Coleman involved. Waddle was mostly invisible in Week 1 with just 2 yards, but he had 138 in Week 2. He won't go off like that every week, but that should be closer to his normal production. Coleman, a rookie, took advantage of injuries to JK Dobbins and RJ Harvey and had 39 yards rushing and 19 yards receiving, and generally looked good. It could become difficult for the Broncos to keep him off the field. The offensive output from Waddle and Coleman, and a much-improved effort from the defense, led to a win over the Jaguars that avoided what would have been a miserable 0-2 start.

"When the sky was falling, I was like, 'Look, this is correctable,'" defensive lineman Zach Allen said, via the team's site .

The Patriots won and they got some downfield passing going, but Drake Maye is still in a slump. He didn't throw a touchdown Sunday and had only 208 yards. His Week 1 struggles can be excused because the Seahawks' defense is incredible. The Steelers' defense isn't on that level and the Patriots were still underwhelming on offense. The Patriots are still figuring out their receiver rotation without A.J. Brown, but the passing offense needs to do more. Maye is 19th in adjusted EPA per play and 10th in success rate, which isn't that bad considering half of his season so far was against Seattle, but it's nowhere near his MVP form of last season.

"You got to be excited and enjoy the win," Maye said, according to Yahoo Sports' Jori Epstein . "But at the same time, you realize that playing like this isn't going to end up with offensively us leading our team to wins."

Edge rusher Dallas Turner seems to be having a breakout in his third season. He leads the NFL in pressures (20), QB hits (8) and PFF's pass rush productivity score. With the Bears at the 12-yard line, trailing 9-3, Turner had a sack on the final play of the game to seal the win. Turner was the 17th pick of the 2024 NFL Draft and he is playing up to that draft status.

"DT being our closer, finishing the whole thing," Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell said after Sunday's win . "DT just keeps showing up."

The Eagles needed to stop a 2-point conversion to beat the Commanders and a last-minute drive with a touchdown in the final seconds to beat the Titans. Those are two of the worst teams in the NFL so far. Life is better at 2-0 but it still has been an uneven start for the Eagles. It's not just an offense learning a new scheme either. The defense is just 22nd in EPA per play allowed and 14th in success rate allowed. The offense is 14th in EPA per play and 27th in success rate. It has been a very mediocre team that made the plays it needed to win two close games. It's early in the season and 2-0 is obviously fine, but don't ignore these warning signs.

There's nothing wrong with losing on the road to a desperate Broncos team. It's tough in the altitude early in the season, and that might have played a factor in the Jaguars blowing a 13-3 second-half lead. Between last season and Week 1, the Jaguars have earned the benefit of the doubt that they're still a very good team despite one loss to a team that went 14-3 last season. One shining light is that receiver Parker Washington has carried over a strong finish from last season. Washington is second in the NFL in target share to only Jaxon Smith-Njigba, according to PFF . Washington is getting 37.5% of the targets despite some good receiver teammates around him. He has turned that into 18 catches for 181 yards through two games. Washington is a rising star.

Rashod Bateman and Mark Andrews both had productive days, but the Ravens missed Zay Flowers in their home loss to the Saints. The Ravens were ahead 17-9 but couldn't put the game away in the fourth quarter and lost in the final two minutes. Taking a deep shot on third-and-1 in a tie game rather than handing it to Derrick Henry didn't work and has been criticized. This type of loss has become a flaw for Baltimore. The Ravens have a league-leading 15 losses after they held a double-digit lead since 2018, the team's site said . That's disappointing but there are positive signs for the Ravens through two weeks. They just need to get their receiver room healthy and do a much better job closing games.

"This is a different team [with] different energy," Andrews said, according to transcripts . "This is not par for the course. We are going to learn from this and continue to be better and capitalize when we need to capitalize."

Kenneth Walker might have the second-biggest impact of anyone in the NFL through two weeks, behind Josh Allen. In Week 1, Walker set a career best by forcing 14 missed tackles. In Week 2, he forced 15 missed tackles . When the Chiefs needed a game-winning drive in overtime, he was involved in five of their six offensive plays. Included in that was a 22-yard gain on a catch that got the Chiefs into easy field-goal range. For the first time in a while, the Chiefs have balance on offense and that's helping Patrick Mahomes.

"It's fun for me, just him running the ball, our offensive line driving off the ball the way that they're driving off," Mahomes said . "It's making defenses have to account for that. I mean, if not, we're going to run the ball for 200 yards or whatever we did the week before, and so you want to be able to do it all."

Is Cincinnati's defense good? It was impressive against Houston. The Bengals paid a big price for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II, giving up the 10th overall pick of the draft to the Giants for him. It looks like he might be worth it. Lawrence had a fantastic game Sunday, including a huge fourth-down stop on RB David Montgomery. The Bengals completely shut down the Texans' run game and Lawrence was the biggest element in that.

The Bengals are fourth in EPA allowed per play. If the defense is going to play anywhere near that level, everyone knows the offense is going to heat up and be among the NFL's best. This is the mix the Bengals have been looking for.

It wasn't outrageous to worry a little about Matthew Stafford after a really poor outing for him in Week 1. He is 38 years old, after all. After Rich Gannon won his first MVP at age 37, like Stafford did last season, he threw only nine more touchdowns the rest of his career. But Monday night looked like vintage Stafford, with 327 yards and four touchdowns. That was without Puka Nacua, who was inactive with a hip injury. The entire performance by the Rams should ease any concerns that might have come up when they were dominated by the 49ers in Australia.

"Obviously we executed at a higher clip, had some explosive plays, which is nice," Stafford told ESPN's Lisa Salters after the game. "To be honest with you, I felt like we could have been more efficient. We had some plays we left out there that I know we can make."

The 49ers got a good runout to start the season. They got the Rams in Australia, when Los Angeles practically blew off that trip by landing the day before the game. Then they got the Dolphins, who have the worst roster in the NFL. They blew out both teams, which shouldn't be taken for granted in the NFL. Their point differential of +42 is dominant. They have had only two negative plays all season, not counting kneeldowns, the fewest for a team this century through two games, according to Doug Clawson of CBS . Brock Purdy is playing well, keeping the offense afloat despite receiver injuries already piling up, and the defense has given up only one touchdown to the Rams and another TD to the Dolphins when they were leading by 29 points in the final minutes. It has been an impressive start.

"Obviously, the scoreboard's been great the last two weeks, but there are so many things we can always get better at and our standard is going to continue to rise," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey said, via 49ers Web Zone . "That's really what we're focused on."

The Seahawks' defense might be even better than last season, and last season's group was phenomenal. Seattle has allowed 17 points in two games. The Seahawks didn't allow a catch longer than 9 yards against the Cardinals in Week 2 and only one run of 10 yards or longer. On the offensive end, Sam Darnold missed Sunday's game and the running game is still in a weird spot with Jadarian Price not fully taking over the RB1 job. It didn't matter because Jaxon Smith-Njigba was fantastic, with 155 yards and three touchdowns.

"We're sitting over there on the sideline, and when he catches the ball, we're just like, 'Man, this guy's a wizard,'" defensive tackle Leonard Williams said about JSN, via the team's site .

It seems like Josh Allen has simply decided that he's going to have a historic season . Allen has at least two passing touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns in each game to start the season. That's only the second time in NFL history a player has scored multiple rushing and passing touchdowns in consecutive games. The first time was Allen in 2024, according to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press . Having a healthy Dalton Kincaid seems to have unlocked a new level in the offense. Kincaid has played well at times but injuries have held him back. Now that he's healthy, he's third in the NFL with 225 receiving yards. Assuming DJ Moore's shoulder injury isn't serious, there's no reason Allen can't set career-high marks this season. And we're talking about a player who has accounted for at least 39 touchdowns in six straight seasons.

articles.title: Browns' Shedeur Sanders Gives Away 500 Backpacks With School Supplies to Youth Students on Video
articles.summary: Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders gave away 500 backpacks filled with school supplies to students at W. H. Kirk Middle School and Caledonia Elementary on Tuesday, per Camryn Justice of News 5 Cleveland.
articles.body:
Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders gave away 500 backpacks filled with school supplies to students at W. H. Kirk Middle School and Caledonia Elementary on Tuesday, per Camryn Justice of News 5 Cleveland.

The children were also treated to food from Pizza Hut and Pammy's Ice Cream as part of the event, via Justice.

Sanders explained why he decided to pick the two schools for the giveaway.

"I chose two schools in East Cleveland because I like going to different places a lot of people wouldn't go and showing a positive side of things because if you just look online, you only see the negativity about parts of East Cleveland and different parts of Cleveland," Sanders said (0:55 mark).

The 24-year-old is in the midst of his second season in Cleveland, operating as the team's backup quarterback behind Deshaun Watson.

Sanders previously appeared in eight games as a rookie, completing 56.6 percent of his passes for 1,400 yards and seven touchdowns to go along with 10 interceptions during his 2025 campaign.

The Browns own a 1-1 record this year and are coming off a 23-19 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday.

As Sanders continues to serve as a depth piece for Cleveland, he took some time to give back to the local community.

articles.title: Giants' Odell Beckham Jr. Shows Support for Jaxson Dart Amid Rumors on QB's Knee Injury
articles.summary: New York Giants veteran wideout Odell Beckham Jr. offered his support to quarterback Jaxson Dart on Tuesday, with reports that the young star suffered a more serious knee injury than initially believed during Monday's 28-6 loss against the Los Angeles Rams.
articles.body:
New York Giants veteran wideout Odell Beckham Jr. offered his support to quarterback Jaxson Dart on Tuesday, with reports that the young star suffered a more serious knee injury than initially believed during Monday's 28-6 loss against the Los Angeles Rams.

NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported Tuesday that Dart "will miss an extended period of time and is facing the possibility of season-ending surgery."

The Giants struck a more optimistic tone on Tuesday night, with the belief that Dart was only dealing with a sprained MCL.

Tuesday's MRI changed the calculus, however.

"We've learned a lot more [about Dart's knee]," Harbaugh said. "When we know what direction we're going to have to go or whatever it might be, we'll announce that. But we don't have that yet, so I don't want to get out over our skis on that."

Any hope of the Giants ending a recent run of futility that has included just one playoff berth in the past nine seasons would almost assuredly be extinguished if Dart was lost for the year. While backup Jameis Winston has plenty of experience as the starter, he's a major step down from Dart.

The 32-year-old was dreadful in relief duty on Monday night, finishing 11-of-27 for 111 yards, no touchdowns, an interception and two sacks taken. The Rams are a tough defense to face, even without Myles Garrett, but Winston didn't inspire much confidence with his performance. Neither do his 114 interceptions in 109 career games.

Teams have rallied behind backup quarterbacks and made playoff runs before, but much of New York's offensive upside seemed predicated on Dart's playmaking ability. That unit now faces a tall task with the possibility of his season being over.

articles.title: Brandin Cooks, 49ers Reportedly Reach Contract Amid Evans and Robinson Injuries, Updated Depth Chart
articles.summary: The San Francisco 49ers are adding some depth to their wide receiver room following Demarcus Robinson's ankle injury, with veteran Mike Evans also nursing a hip injury.
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers are adding some depth to their wide receiver room following Demarcus Robinson's ankle injury , with veteran Mike Evans also nursing a hip injury .

Per ESPN's Adam Schefter, the Niners have signed veteran Brandin Cooks to their practice squad to get him up to speed before bringing him onto the roster.

Cooks was a first-round draft pick by the New Orleans Saints in 2014 and has also spent time with the New England Patriots, Los Angeles Rams, Houston Texans, Dallas Cowboys and Buffalo Bills.

He's recorded six seasons with 1,000-plus receiving yards: two in New Orleans, one in New England, one in Los Angeles and two in Houston, his most recent of which came in 2021.

He returned to the Saints last season but was cut in November after requesting to be released. He finished the season with the Bills. Across 15 games last year, he had 279 yards on 24 receptions.

Cooks is far from an elite receiver at 32 years old, but the Niners need all the help they can get after having their wide receiver room decimated by injuries already this year.

Ricky Pearsall underwent season-ending surgery to repair his PCL before the season even started, eliminating a player who was set to be one of Brock Purdy's key targets.

De'Zhaun Stribling suffered an ankle injury in Week 1, and he'll miss at least 10 weeks after undergoing surgery. Robinson is looking at missed time after a high-ankle sprain, and Evans is questionable heading into Week 3 because of a hip injury.

The 49ers figure to be playoff contenders after a 2-0 start that included a win over the Los Angeles Rams, but all the injuries piling up mean they'll have to stay afloat until they can get everyone healthy.

Cooks will look to aid the offense and perhaps earn a larger role even when key receivers return.

articles.title: Davante Adams Talks Matthew Stafford's Place Among NFL GOATs After Rams' Win vs. Giants
articles.summary: Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Davante Adams explained why he believes that teammate Matthew Stafford should be considered one of the greatest quarterbacks in NFL history.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Davante Adams explained why he believes that teammate Matthew Stafford should be considered one of the greatest quarterbacks in NFL history.

"Well to be honest, I think we'd be talking about him as maybe the greatest quarterback of all time," Adams said during a Tuesday appearance on the Pat McAfee Show (9:26 mark). "The tough part about being a quarterback in this league is so much of your success and how good you are, how legendary you'll become, is based off of winning. Obviously you start in a place like Detroit where they weren't winning at the rate that the Rams have been since he's been here. Since 2021."

"If his whole career had been here with a guy like Sean they'd be saying, 'Is this guy literally the best quarterback that's ever played?' So winning games obviously helps a lot of that," he added. "I always respect the guys that can do it consistently for a really long time."

Stafford and Adams are beginning their second season as teammates, coming off a 28-6 win over the New York Giants on Monday night.

Stafford finished 22-of-31 for 327 yards and four touchdowns compared to one interception.

Adams was Stafford's top target against New York, hauling in a game-high eight receptions for 195 yards and two scores.

With an 11-yard touchdown catch by Adams in the third quarter of the game, Stafford moved into No. 6 on the NFL's all-time passing touchdowns leaderboard .

The veteran signal-caller also sits at No. 6 on the league's all-time passing yards list .

Stafford started his career on the Detroit Lions from 2009-20, but made just three playoff appearances during his 12 seasons with the team.

Since joining forces with the Rams and head coach Sean McVay in 2021, Stafford has advanced to the playoffs four times. He's also won a Super Bowl title to go along with an MVP honor.

Stafford owned a 74-90-1 record as a starter in Detroit compared to a 47-29 record with Los Angeles.

articles.title: Three Word Game: Three words to describe every NFL team so far this season ahead of Week 3
articles.summary: Kenneth Walker leads the NFL in rushing as the Kansas City Chiefs boast the league's top-ranked offense, while the Detroit Lions' defense allows 71 points.
articles.body: In life, it often takes just three words to tell a story. NFL teams are no different. Today, we play to the OutKick-famous Three-Word Game to describe every NFL team after two weeks: Detroit Lions (1-1): Defense is putrid. The Lions’ defense ranks 31st in points and yards allowed. They have allowed 71 points through two games. The secondary is a mess and cannot pressure the quarterback. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard’s seat could and should get hot quickly. Kansas City Chiefs (2-0): They are back. The Chiefs have had an average offense over the past three seasons. Not this year. Through two games, Kansas City has the NFL’s top-ranked offense. Free-agent addition Kenneth Walker has been the biggest move of the offseason. He leads the NFL in rushing yards (290) and all-purpose yards (369). There are reasonable concerns about whether the Chiefs can sustain this pace, especially with left tackle Josh Simmons still out under mysterious circumstances. For now, the Chiefs look back to their old ways. New York Giants (1-1): Season’s probably over. After Week 1, the Giants looked like a playoff team and a potential dark-horse contender. After Week 2, that all seems like a distant memory. ESPN reported Tuesday that quarterback Jaxson Dart’s knee injury is worse than expected and that he is likely to miss the rest of the season. Backup Jameis Winston hardly looked playable in relief Monday night against the Rams. Miami Dolphins (0-2): Arch? Chambliss? Mensah? Challenge: Name five players on the Miami Dolphins. MIAMI DOLPHINS ENTER FULL REBUILD WITH MALIK WILLIS AT QUARTERBACK AND JEFF HAFLEY AS HEAD COACH We can’t either. The Dolphins’ roster is the least talented in recent memory. It’s difficult to envision them missing out on one of the top quarterbacks in what is expected to be an elite 2027 draft class. The options could include Arch Manning, Trinidad Chambliss or keeping Hurricanes quarterback Darian Mensah in Miami. San Francisco 49ers (2-0): Better than expected. The 49ers were not frequently mentioned among the NFL’s best teams entering the season. Through two weeks, they are clearly among them. Remember, this team entered Week 18 last season with a chance to earn the NFC’s No. 1 seed despite injuries to multiple All-Pro players. If San Francisco can remain reasonably healthy, it should again contend for the top seed. This roster is still loaded. Cleveland Browns (1-1): Well, they won. In the biggest upset of the season, the Browns edged the Buccaneers on Sunday after a lengthy late-fourth-quarter weather delay. Browns fans may have preferred another poor performance from Deshaun Watson. Instead, his 238-yard, two-touchdown, zero-interception performance will likely buy him at least a few more weeks as the starter. FROM THE CHARGERS TO THE COLTS AND FALCONS, WHICH OF THE NFL'S EIGHT WINLESS TEAMS ARE ALREADY IN PANIC MODE Buffalo Bills (2-0): No, it’s different. Yes, the Bills have been Super Bowl champions in September for most of Josh Allen’s career, only to lose in heartbreaking fashion in January. But this time does feel different. Under head coach Joe Brady, Buffalo has the NFL’s highest-scoring offense and has turned tight end Dalton Kincaid into the league’s best pass-catching option. The Bills may not have the marquee names of the Rams, but their roster is among the league’s most complete. Notably, edge rusher Greg Rousseau leads the NFL with four sacks and may have elevated his game from good to great. Atlanta Falcons (0-2): Can’t flex yet. Unfortunately, networks cannot flex games out of prime time this early in the season. Therefore, the Falcons will be forced to perform on national television each of the next three weeks. Minnesota Vikings (2-0): The Northern favorites. The Vikings entered the season with the lowest odds of winning what was expected to be a vaunted NFC North. Suddenly, concerns about the Lions’ defense, the Packers’ roster and Caleb Williams’ health have made Minnesota the betting favorite to win the division. Further, the Vikings have the talent to justify it. Las Vegas Raiders (2-0): Just LIKE that. Just like that, the Raiders are 2-0 and have formed the NFL’s best pass-blocking line, according to ESPN Stats & Information. Brock Bowers, the Raiders’ best player, is also expected to make his season debut Sunday. The schedule gets tougher from here. Las Vegas’ next five opponents are the Saints, Chiefs, Patriots, Bills and Rams. Winning two of those matchups would seem like a victory for this team. Houston Texans (0-2): Not worried, yet. The Texans started 0-3 last season and finished 12-5. There is no reason to panic just yet. That said, Houston’s highly acclaimed defense has not been nearly as strong this season. The Texans rank 20th in yards allowed and 24th in points allowed. Playing Josh Allen and Joe Burrow in consecutive weeks can do that to a defense. But C.J. Stroud is not good enough to lead this team into the postseason if the defense is anything short of dominant. Philadelphia Eagles (2-0): Fly, Eagles … fly? The good news: The Eagles are 2-0. The bad news: They do not look particularly effective on either side of the ball. The jury is still out in Philadelphia. Fortunately, the Eagles may face the Bears on Monday with Case Keenum starting at quarterback. Los Angeles Rams (1-1): Super Bowl favorites. Forget what happened in Australia. The Rams have the best roster in the NFL. Aaron Donald looked like Aaron Donald on Monday night. Myles Garrett, Puka Nacua and Donald have not even shared the field yet. Barring injury, the Rams should remain Super Bowl favorites throughout the season. Tennessee Titans (0-2): So, so close. The Titans looked like they had the Eagles, then they didn’t. Cam Ward still has a ways to go. It’s early, but so far, Carnell Tate has not lived up to his status as the fourth overall pick. Still, Tennessee should have an opportunity to win its first game this week against a Jaxson Dart-less Giants team. Dallas Cowboys (1-1): Waiting to see. The Dallas Cowboys have as good an offense as any team in the NFL. The question is how much last year’s historically bad defense has improved. They looked better Sunday against the Commanders once Daniels went down. Through two games, the team has yet to record a sack. This team could go either way. Carolina Panthers (1-1): Bryce is cooking. Imagine telling anyone after their rookie seasons that Bryce Young would be better than Stroud. And yet, that is the case after the past two seasons. The Panthers have scored 71 points in two games. That’s second-best in the NFL. Seattle Seahawks (2-0): They can repeat. Few teams received less hype about potentially repeating as Super Bowl champions in the offseason than the Seattle Seahawks. But they can. The roster is well-rounded, they play fierce defense, and Jaxon Smith-Njigba is nearly unguardable. The Seahawks have even turned Drew Lock into a serviceable quarterback this season. That’s impressive. Baltimore Ravens (1-1): Not this again. For what seems like the fifth year in a row, the Ravens dominated Week 1, and the national media rushed to anoint them the top team in the AFC and Lamar Jackson the MVP frontrunner. Then, as usual, the team suffered a major letdown in Week 2 against the Saints, culminating in a game-losing interception thrown by Jackson. They never learn. They being the media. Denver Broncos (1-1): Week 1 lies. As always, Week 1 lies to us. Week 1 told us the Denver Broncos were a poorly coached team with holes on both sides of the ball. Week 2 tends to be more truthful and showed us the opposite. The Denver Broncos are really good. The addition of Jaylen Waddle showed on Sunday. New York Jets (1-1): Maybe not hopeless. The Jets are not good, but they are not completely hopeless, either. That qualifies as progress in New York. They should be 2-0. Cincinnati Bengals (2-0): They play defense. The Bengals deviated from strategy this offseason and paid for a defense. It’s working. Two weeks in, the Bengals are pressuring the quarterback and forcing teams off the field. If that continues, the Bengals can beat anyone. Now, if Joe Burrow could stay healthy … Arizona Cardinals (1-1): The real LaFleur. The Cardinals are, dare we say, competitive. Between Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love and Michael Wilson, Arizona has a puncher’s chance against most opponents. First-year coach Mike LaFleur is impressive. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1): Same old Steelers. Pittsburgh remains well-coached, physical, and offensively limited. The Steelers are exactly what everyone expected and exactly what they seemingly are every season. They are also so boring to watch. Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1): Another false alarm. The Jaguars briefly looked like a contender. Then reality returned. Jacksonville still has too many holes to be taken seriously. Chicago Bears (1-1): The crisis averted. It sounds like Caleb Williams will miss a game or two because of a hamstring injury. But if you told the Bears that and a week of crying-Caleb memes was the worst-case scenario after how bad his injury looked, they would take it. The Bears will be fine. Los Angeles Chargers (0-2): Not getting better. The Chargers are 0-2. The offense and defense look confused. The offensive line is once again a weakness. Jim Harbaugh looks befuddled on the sideline. None of it makes much sense. Worst of all, the Chargers’ next seven opponents are the Buffalo Bills, Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Kansas City Chiefs, Los Angeles Rams, Houston Texans, and Baltimore Ravens. What’s the best-case scenario here? A 1-8 start? New England Patriots (1-1): Much-improved defense. The Patriots’ offense has struggled. A.J. Brown is hurt, and stud right guard Mike Onwenu is out for the season. However, the defense is much improved from last season. The team has allowed only 16 points through two games against the Seahawks and Steelers. Drake Maye must play better, though. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-2): Very, very disappointing? Two weeks into this season, the Bucks are one of the NFL's biggest disappointments. They lost to the Browns. The talent is there, but they need to win three of their next five against the Vikings, Packers, Cowboys, Steelers, and Panthers. We aren't sure they will do it. Green Bay Packers (1-1): Well, they survived. The Packers survived a double-digit deficit to the Jets on Sunday to avoid a 0-2 start. In doing so, Green Bay became the first team since 1941 to win a game while recording fewer than 200 yards of offense, 100-plus penalty yards and a negative turnover margin. The team is not clicking and may need to keep surviving until Micah Parsons and Josh Jacobs return. Indianapolis Colts (0-2): Last-ranked defense. The Colts’ offense was impressive in an overtime loss to the Chiefs. However, the defense has been horrendous. Through two weeks, the Colts’ defense has given up 1,029 total yards, which ranks last in the NFL, along with 675 passing yards, also last, 354 rushing yards, second-to-last, and 74 points, last. That’s a problem. New Orleans Saints (1-1): No Shoughs given. The Saints might have the best quarterback most of the public has never heard of: Tyler Shough. He leads the league in passing yards and firmly outplayed Lamar Jackson head-to-head Sunday. The touted rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson is expected to make his season debut next month, giving Shough another option. In the NFC South, the Saints are a playoff-caliber team — and one with firepower. Washington Commanders (0-2): He’s hurt again. Jayden Daniels is hurt again. This roster isn’t good enough to overcome annual injuries to a quarterback who makes everything work.
